entities.name: Juan de Borja Lanzol de Romaní, el mayor
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Juan de Borja Lanzol (Llançol) de Romaní, el mayor, born into the prominent Valencian Borja family, rose to significant ecclesiastical power as the first of ten cardinal-nephews elevated by his cousin's father, Pope Alexander VI (Rodrigo Borgia). Elevated to the cardinalate on 31 August 1492, just weeks after Alexander VI's election, Borja Lanzol's rapid ascent exemplifies the pervasive nepotism and strategic consolidation of power characteristic of the Renaissance Papacy. His career, though relatively short, was deeply intertwined with the ambitions of the Borgia family, leveraging his familial ties to secure influence within the Roman Curia and across the Papal States.

As Cardinal-Deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata and later Cardinal-Priest of Santa Susanna, Juan de Borja Lanzol held several key administrative and diplomatic roles. He served as the Archbishop of Monreale in Sicily from 1492 until his death, a lucrative appointment that provided substantial income and influence. Beyond his ecclesiastical duties, he acted as a trusted advisor and representative for Pope Alexander VI, participating in critical diplomatic missions, including negotiations related to the Italian Wars and the intricate web of alliances and rivalries that defined late 15th-century European politics. His elevation was a clear signal of Alexander VI's intent to surround himself with loyal family members to secure his pontificate.

entities.summary:
Juan de Borja Lanzol de Romaní, el mayor, a scion of the influential Borja (Borgia) family, emerged as a significant figure in the Renaissance Papacy, primarily through his elevation to the cardinalate by his cousin, Pope Alexander VI (Rodrigo Borja). Born in Xàtiva in 1446, he embodied the era's pervasive practice of nepotism, serving as the first of ten cardinal-nephews appointed by Alexander VI. His career intertwined with the ambitious political and ecclesiastical designs of the Borgia pontificate, deeply impacting the administrative landscape of the Holy See and the secular power dynamics within the Papal States during the late 15th and early 16th centuries.

Elevated to cardinal on August 31, 1492, just weeks after Alexander VI's election, Juan de Borja quickly accumulated numerous ecclesiastical offices and benefices, including the Archbishopric of Monreale (1492), the Bishopric of Melfi (1492), and the Governorship of Rome (1493). He played a direct role in the pope's efforts to consolidate power, often acting as a trusted envoy and administrator. For instance, he participated in the negotiations with Charles VIII of France during the First Italian War (1494-1498), seeking to protect the Papal States from foreign encroachment while navigating complex alliances and betrayals typical of the period.

His meteoric rise and the accumulation of wealth and power underscored the secularization of the papacy under Alexander VI, setting a precedent for the subsequent, even more audacious, appointments within the Borja family, most notably Cesare Borgia. Juan de Borja's tenure as cardinal contributed to the perception of the Church as a temporal power, driven by dynastic ambition rather than purely spiritual concerns. His influence helped solidify the Borja family's grip on both ecclesiastical and secular authority, leaving an indelible mark on the political map of Italy and the internal structure of the Roman Curia.
